title: Foot-in-the-Door
description: Asking for a tiny, easy favor to get a 'yes', then immediately following up with a large request.

sections.title: Quick Understanding
sections.content: Get them to say a microscopic 'yes' first. Asking for a tiny, extremely easy favor gets your foot in the door, making them statistically much more likely to say yes to the huge, real request that follows.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Consistency. Once we say yes to the small favor, our internal self-image shifts. We now see ourselves as 'the specific type of person who supports this cause.' To stay internally consistent with that new identity, we say yes to the big favor.

sections.title: Real-Life Examples
content: Charity: 'Can you sign this free petition immediately?' -> 'Great, can you donate $20?'
Sales: Offering a perfectly free 30-day trial requiring setup, then asking for a $100/mo subscription.
Workplace: 'Can you just read the very first paragraph of this report?' -> 'Can you finish it for me?'
Daily Life: A neighbor asks to borrow a cup of sugar. A week later, they ask to borrow your car.

sections.title: What It Looks Like
content: Street Fundraiser: 'Excuse me, do you believe children should have clean water?'
Pedestrian: 'Yes, of course.'
Street Fundraiser: 'Awesome, can you just sign this absolutely free petition?'
Pedestrian: (Signs it) 'Sure.'
Street Fundraiser: 'Thank you! If everyone who signed gave just $5, we could build a well today. Can I count on your $5?'

sections.title: Pattern Recognition
content: A request so incredibly small and easy it feels socially awkward to say no.
A rapid series of escalating 'yes' questions.
Someone asking for your 'opinion' or a 'signature' before ever mentioning money.

sections.title: Ethical Uses
sections.content: Easing people into positive, intimidating habits. E.g., getting someone to jog for just 5 minutes instead of 5 miles to build initial momentum.

sections.title: Manipulative Uses
sections.content: Tricking people into massive financial commitments by hiding the true request. Upselling aggressively once the person is mentally trapped by their own compliance.

sections.title: Red Flags
content: A completely context-free, microscopic request from a stranger.
Being casually asked to make a 'small verbal commitment' (like 'Are you an open-minded person?').
The immediate, sharp pivot from a free favor directly to a paid request.

sections.title: Defense Strategies
content: Judge the large request completely independently of the small favor.
Recognize the foot-in-the-door tactic and refuse the absolute first small favor if you suspect a trap.
Tell them explicitly: 'I will sign the petition, but I will categorically not give money.'

sections.title: Mistakes People Make
content: Naively thinking the small favor is the complete end of the interaction.
Feeling hypocritical if they say no to the big favor after saying yes to the small one.

sections.title: Case Study
sections.content: Researchers knocked on doors asking residents to place a massive, ugly 'Drive Carefully' billboard on their front lawn. Only 17% agreed. In a second group, they first asked residents to place a tiny 3-inch 'Be a Safe Driver' sticker in their window. Almost everyone agreed. Two weeks later, they asked that second group about the massive ugly billboard. 76% agreed. The small sticker completely changed their identity.

sections.title: Key Lessons
content: 1. The tiny 'yes' alters human identity.
2. Compliance deeply breeds more compliance.
3. Beware the completely microscopic favor.
4. It is perfectly fine to stop saying yes at any time.
